paragraphs: Even after my study abroad at Korea University was decided, I continued studying English, centring on English conversation. After it was decided that I could do clerkships in orthopedics and emergency medicine, I also worked on studying medicine in English and Japanese, centring on those fields. A senior who had studied at Korea University had told me that not being able to speak Korean would not hinder the clerkship, so I did not study it in particular. On practical matters, even two months before departure there was no reply to emails from the other side, and it could not be confirmed until one month before whether the clerkship could take place, so booking flights and lodging and handling insurance procedures had to be done at the last minute, which was a struggle.

In the orthopedic clerkship, I mainly observed surgery. On the first day, by chance, two orthopedic surgeons from Japan had come to observe, and I received supplementary explanations not only from the Korea University doctors but also from those doctors, which was very educational. As a difference between surgery in Japan and Korea, the Japanese doctors said that awareness of cleanliness is somewhat lower than in Japan but, instead, the time per operation is very short, and they said they do operations at a pace unthinkable in Japan, five or six in a day. However, the operating room was extremely cold, and I caught a cold and had to be absent the next day. In the emergency medicine clerkship, I was able to see the actual state of emergency care in Korea. In Korea, because of the strike, there are currently no residents in the hospitals, and emergency care seemed to be especially affected. At Korea University Hospital, although three rooms with about 15 beds each had been prepared according to the triage colours, because of staff shortages only one room was used, and patients were gathered in that room regardless of triage colour. I was also told that the hospital accepted only severely ill patients. Also, in Korea, to avoid unnecessary use of ambulances, a fee is charged when an ambulance is used for a mild condition, and I felt that Japan should also introduce a similar system.

On days off I went sightseeing at Seoul Tower and Panmunjom. At Panmunjom I could actually look at North Korea and learn about the history of conflict and dialogue with North Korea, which was very interesting. Korean food was all very delicious, and I had no trouble with food.
